 When I moved to Utah as a student a decade ago, I was alarmed to be handed a survival pack upon reaching my dorm. These were supplies to help me, should 'The Big One' strike. This cataclysmic confluence of earthquakes and tsunamis across the San Andreas fault was, I was told, long overdue, and could plunge half of the country into a Fallout -like situationship for a little while.
 Well, now I'm back living in the UK, and apparently the apocalypse is coming for us here too: the government in Blighty has told us to stock up on tinned beans and survival supplies, and has even put out an emergency checklist of kit we should have prepared .
 Among the obvious items on the list (tinned food to last three days; three liters of bottled water per person for each day we're stuck; blankets), the government advises you to own an FM radio, ideally a battery-powered or wind-up (see also: hand-crank) one. And retailers are reporting that many such models are selling out.
 Latest Videos From TechRadar 
 Watch full video here: 
 For people confused about this: an FM radio is an old gadget from before Spotify and podcasts existed, which lets you tune into broadcasts put out by various companies (you could choose between dry BBC talk shows or countless playlists of awful music, punctuated by the most annoying ads).
 I guess the government thinks people will start listening to the radio again if a 28 Days Later situation does arise; maybe they'll give you important broadcasts on the news, a droll hour-long report on a book from 50 years ago, or the same three pop songs on repeat.

 Philips TAR1609/00

It's looking a little bit hard to buy, likely because of the current rush on demand, but its UK Amazon listing is here for when stock returns.  For photographers, choosing the best rechargeable batteries can make a real difference to a shoot. Modern speedlights and wireless flash triggers can be demanding, needing not only strong capacity but also reliable, consistent power delivery. The best rechargeable batteries are more than capable of meeting these demands, while also working out far cheaper than disposable cells over time.
 Better still, the latest rechargeable batteries have largely overcome one of the biggest frustrations of older cells: self-discharge. Some options can now hold their charge for months, or even years, when stored correctly. Having tested countless flashes and batteries, I’ve found that modern NiMH rechargeable AA batteries are a dependable choice not only for photography kits, but also for everyday electronics such as torches, remotes, and other household devices.
 NiMH, or Nickel-Metal Hydride, batteries remain the gold standard for most photographic uses, but newer Li-ion rechargeable AA batteries are starting to challenge that position. Their key advantage is a 1.5V output, matching conventional alkaline batteries rather than the 1.2V typically delivered by NiMH cells. For that reason, I’ve included this newer type as well, at number five on the list.
 And if you need smaller cells, take a look at our separate guide to the best AAA rechargeable batteries.

 How to choose the best rechargeable batteries 
 When choosing the best rechargeable batteries, I would generally recommend NiMH, or Nickel-Metal Hydride, cells. These became popular in the 1990s because they offered higher capacities than older NiCad, or Nickel-Cadmium, batteries, while also avoiding the memory effect that meant NiCad cells needed to be fully discharged before being recharged.
 That said, early NiMH batteries, and some cheaper options still available today, can lose their charge within a few weeks even when not being used. The batteries we have recommended above are designed to reduce that problem, making them much more dependable for photography and everyday use. The right choice will depend on what matters most to you, whether that is overall capacity, the number of recharge cycles, or value for money.
 Battery capacity is measured in milliampere-hours, or mAh, which shows how much electrical power the battery can hold over time. In general, a higher mAh rating means the battery will last longer between charges, although very high-capacity batteries may offer fewer recharge cycles over their lifetime.

 How we tested the best rechargeable AA batteries 
 I evaluated all the AA batteries in this guide through hands-on, real-world testing, using them in speedlights like the Nikon Speedlight SB-700 , one of the best flashguns . I assessed their recycle speed by performing at least 300 full-power flashes and repeating the test several months later, after multiple recharges. I also examined how quickly they charge and whether the battery life matches the manufacturer's claims. To finalize our recommendations, we compared our results with stated specifications and customer reviews, selecting the best rechargeable AA batteries for various needs, including value and high-capacity options.

 FAQs 
 Why do rechargeable batteries suddenly run out of power? 
 Alkaline batteries have a relatively consistent discharge rate during use. For instance, when used in a flashgun, the recycle time between flashes will gradually increase. In contrast, NiMH batteries provide a more stable voltage throughout most of their discharge cycle, but the voltage drops off quickly near the end, when they are nearly depleted.
 Why does the charge indicator not show full when I insert fresh rechargeable batteries?
 When fresh, alkaline batteries have a potential difference of 1.5V across their electrodes. In contrast, NiMH batteries provide a lower 1.2V, even when fully charged. As a result, devices with an integrated volt meter may show a lower reading when using NiMH batteries.
 Do I need to fully discharge NiMH batteries before recharging them? 
 Unlike older NiCad (Nickel Cadmium) rechargeable batteries, NiMH batteries don’t suffer from a ‘memory effect’. This means that there’s no need to fully discharge them before recharging.
 What’s the best quantity of rechargeable batteries to buy?
 As with anything, it only pays to buy as many as you need. However, NiMH is an effective replacement for regular (non-rechargeable) alkaline AA batteries in most devices and, like most things, if you buy in larger quantities, there are often significant savings to be made.
 What’s the best way to store rechargeable batteries when not in use?
 Ideally, rechargeable batteries should be stored in a cool, dry place. Theoretically, the colder the better, but it’s best not to store them in a refrigerator to avoid the risk of condensation when you take them out for use.
 Can I use any charging device for my rechargeable batteries?
 Most battery manufacturers recommend using their own-brand chargers, and you can typically purchase the charger and AA cells together in a kit. While third-party chargers are generally safe, it's best to avoid "fast chargers," as they can reduce the battery's lifespan and lead to issues such as overheating or leakage.  Never charge alkaline, lithium-primary or other non-rechargeable batteries in a NiMH charger.
 In a device using batteries in series, keep matched cells as a labeled set; charge and use them together.

 Safe charging checklist
 Confirm the cells are rechargeable NiMH, not alkaline or lithium primary batteries.
 Match the polarity markings and keep ventilation around the charger.
 Do not mix chemistries, substantially different capacities, or old and new cells in one device or charge cycle.
 For devices using batteries in series, buy matched cells together, label them as a set, and charge and use that set together.
 Stop using any cell that becomes unusually hot, leaks, swells, smells abnormal or repeatedly fails to charge.
 Recycle depleted rechargeables through an appropriate local battery program rather than household trash where prohibited.
 IKEA’s safety guidance also warns against deforming, dismantling, opening, short-circuiting, heating or immersing batteries, and against skin or eye contact with leaking material.
 Common compatibility and performance problems
 “Low battery” appears too soon
 The device may measure voltage rather than remaining capacity. A NiMH cell can still have useful energy after a voltage-based warning. If the device shuts down repeatedly, consult its manual; a supported 1.5V lithium rechargeable or non-rechargeable battery may be necessary.
 Cells are used in series
 Two or more cells in series should be a matched, labeled set. Do not add a new cell to an older one. If one cell becomes defective, replace the complete set; the weakest cell can be over-discharged and may make the whole pack appear faulty.
 Cold weather
 All battery chemistries lose performance as temperature falls. Check the model’s specified operating and storage limits instead of assuming normal runtime outdoors in freezing conditions.
 USB-rechargeable AA batteries
 Integrated USB cells are convenient, but their electronics can alter fit, require a particular cable and make replacement impossible after the internal battery ages. They are best treated as a convenience option, not a default replacement for standard NiMH cells.

 Lowest practical price: IKEA LADDA 1900, if IKEA access and stock are convenient.

 Voltage problem: investigate a reputable 1.5V lithium rechargeable only after checking the device manual and charger requirements.
 Charger: choose individual-slot NiMH charging with automatic termination.

 Which Devices Should Use Rechargeables (and Which Shouldn’t)?
 NiMH rechargeables are rated at 1.2 volts, against 1.5 volts for a fresh alkaline cell. Most devices run fine on them, but a few are designed around alkaline. 
 Switch these first: compatible devices that go through disposable batteries often, such as game controllers, toys, flashlights and camera flashes. How many disposables each recharge replaces depends on the device.

 Limitation: Panasonic optimizes it for eneloop cells. It is for NiMH cells only: never put alkaline, single-use lithium or 1.5 V USB-rechargeable lithium AAs in a NiMH charger.
 Don’t Trust the Biggest mAh Number
 A higher mAh number on the wrapper doesn’t guarantee more runtime. In one independent test (January 2025, on samples EBL supplied), eight white EBL 2800 mAh AA cells measured 1,950 to 2,169 mAh, an average of 2,045 mAh or about 27% below their rating, while eight of the brand’s “Year of the Dragon” cells averaged 2,576 mAh, about 92%. Those results describe those samples, not every high-mAh AA, but they are why we didn’t include the white cells.
 Look for a “minimum” capacity. eneloop lists both minimum and typical mAh; a single round number tells you less.
 Standard AA NiMH is about 2,000 mAh. Higher-capacity cells like eneloop pro (2,500 mAh minimum) are rated for far fewer recharges, so be skeptical of cheap cells that claim both very high capacity and very long life.
 Low self-discharge is about storage, not capacity. LSD cells are designed to keep their charge on the shelf for months to years.
 How to Charge and Care for Rechargeable Batteries
 Use a NiMH charger with individual slots. Chargers that monitor each cell (like the CC17 and CC63) stop each one when it is full. Never charge alkaline batteries.
 Charge indoors, within the charger’s temperature range. eneloop cells can be used in the cold (the listing says down to -4°F), but charge them indoors at the temperatures the charger’s manual gives. Remove charged cells and unplug the charger when you’re done.
 Top up before storage. LSD cells are designed to sit charged, so charge them before they go in a drawer or an emergency kit, store them cool and dry, and check emergency spares now and then.
 Stop using damaged or leaking cells. Ask the maker or your household hazardous waste program how to handle them; ordinary collection boxes may not accept damaged batteries.
 Are Rechargeable Batteries Better for the Environment?
 Yes, if you recharge them many times. According to a 2016 life-cycle study by Dolci and colleagues , under the study’s assumptions about 50 charge cycles was enough for rechargeable batteries to clearly reduce the assessed environmental impacts compared with disposables, in every category except ozone depletion. That is not a universal break-even point. A battery that sits in a drawer and is charged twice saves little. So buy rechargeables for the devices you actually use, and keep them in use.
 Recycle them correctly. EPA says rechargeable batteries, including NiMH and lithium-ion, should not go in household trash or municipal recycling bins. Take them to a battery recycler, a retailer take-back program or a household hazardous waste collection site, and tape the terminals or bag each battery separately first. The Battery Network’s drop-off locator lists drop-off sites by ZIP code. EPA adds that in most communities alkaline batteries can go in household trash, but it recommends sending them to battery recyclers or checking local rules.
 Fire safety: loose batteries with exposed terminals can short-circuit against keys, coins or other batteries. Store spares in a case or their packaging, and tape the terminals of dead batteries before you collect them for recycling.
 Notes for UK and EU Readers
 In the UK, government guidance ( GOV.UK ) says shops that sell 32 kg or more of portable batteries a year must take back used portable batteries free of charge, so many supermarkets have a collection box. In the EU, the EU Batteries Regulation 2023/1542 sets rising collection targets for portable batteries. The product links on this page go to Amazon US; eneloop and other NiMH cells are widely sold by UK and EU retailers.

 Frequently Asked Questions
 What are the best rechargeable batteries?
 For most homes, our pick (based on maker specs and listings, not our own tests) is the Panasonic eneloop AA 8-pack, with the eneloop AAA pack for remotes, the eneloop CC17 starter kit if you need a charger, and Amazon Basics AA as the budget pick.
 Are rechargeable batteries worth it?
 Yes in compatible devices that go through batteries often, such as game controllers, toys and flashlights. A 2016 life-cycle study found that, under its assumptions, about 50 charge cycles clearly reduced the assessed environmental impacts compared with disposables, except ozone depletion. In a clock that needs new batteries once a year, the benefit is small.
 Can I use rechargeable batteries in everything?
 No. Most devices work on 1.2 V NiMH cells, but some smart locks, some thermostats and smoke alarms are designed for alkaline or lithium. Schlage, for example, doesn’t recommend rechargeables in its residential locks. Check the device manual, and in smoke alarms use only the battery the alarm specifies.
 How many times can you recharge a battery?
 It depends on the cell and how you use it. Panasonic’s listings rate standard eneloop for up to 2,100 recharges and eneloop pro for up to 500 under lab conditions; Amazon Basics AA lists up to 1,000. Real-world life is usually shorter and depends on how you use and charge them.
 What is a low self-discharge battery?
 A NiMH battery designed to hold its charge in storage, so it can be used straight from the drawer like an alkaline. eneloop’s listing claims up to 70% of the charge after 10 years in storage.
 How do I dispose of rechargeable batteries?
 Don’t put them in the trash or curbside recycling. Tape the terminals or bag each battery, then take them to a battery recycler, a retailer take-back program or a household hazardous waste site; The Battery Network’s locator lists sites by ZIP code.
 The Bottom Line
 For most homes, start with the Panasonic eneloop AA 8-pack and the eneloop AAA 8-pack , or the CC17 starter kit if you need a charger; choose Amazon Basics AA to spend less up front. Put them in compatible devices that go through batteries often, keep alkaline or lithium where the manual asks for it, and recycle every cell at the end of its life.

 Quick picks
 Three batteries, three different trade-offs. 
 The Eneloop standard is the preparedness battery. The Eneloop Pro is the capacity battery. The EBL 2800 is the budget battery. Each wins decisively in its lane. Most households should start with the first.

 All batteries are 1.2V NiMH. Capacity and self-discharge figures are from manufacturer specifications. Self-discharge is measured at 20 C (68 F) per IEC 61951-2. Actual retention varies with storage temperature and humidity.
 How we chose
 Self-discharge is the only spec that matters in a drawer. 
 Most rechargeable battery comparisons sort by capacity. More milliamp-hours sounds better. But for emergency preparedness, the question is not how long a battery lasts in use. The question is whether it has any charge at all when you grab it in the dark.
 Older NiMH batteries lost most of their charge within weeks. You would charge them, put them away, and find them dead a month later. Panasonic's Eneloop line solved this problem in 2005, and the current fifth-generation cells have pushed it to an extreme: 70% retention after 10 years at 20 C, verified against the IEC 61951-2 testing standard. That is not marketing. That is a testable, repeatable physical property of the improved metal-hydride alloy lattice inside the cell.
 The Eneloop Pro trades some of that shelf stability for higher capacity: 2,550mAh versus 2,000mAh, but retention drops to 85% after one year with no published multi-year figure. The cycle life drops from 2,100 to 500. For a flashlight you use every weekend and recharge regularly, the Pro makes sense. For a flashlight stored in an emergency kit, the standard Eneloop is the better battery despite having less capacity on paper.
 EBL's 2,800mAh cells offer the highest capacity at the lowest price. Their published retention is 80% after three years, which positions them between the two Eneloops. Independent testing by outlets like CNN Underscored and eneloop101.com has confirmed that EBL cells deliver close to their rated capacity, though they tend to lose capacity slightly faster over many cycles than Eneloops do. For filling a large household with rechargeables on a budget, EBL is a legitimate choice.
 We weighted self-discharge first, cycle life second, and raw capacity third. That order is why the standard Eneloop, with the lowest capacity of the three, earns Our Pick. The battery that is ready after five years in a kitchen drawer is worth more than the battery that runs 40% longer but might be dead when you reach for it.
 What you should know
 The practical details behind the specs. 
 NiMH runs at 1.2V, not 1.5V
 All three batteries in this comparison are NiMH chemistry with a nominal voltage of 1.2V, compared to 1.5V for disposable alkaline. In practice, most devices handle this fine. A fresh alkaline battery starts at 1.5V and drops steadily to about 1.0V before it is useless. A NiMH cell holds a flat 1.2V for most of its discharge, then drops off sharply at the end. The total energy delivered is comparable. A few devices with strict voltage requirements may not work well with 1.2V cells. If that is a concern, USB-C rechargeable lithium-ion AAs from brands like Pale Blue deliver a true 1.5V, though at a higher price per cell and with fewer cycles.
 Why alkaline batteries leak and NiMH batteries do not
 Alkaline batteries use potassium hydroxide as an electrolyte. When the battery is deeply discharged or left in a device for months, that electrolyte can leak out and corrode the battery contacts, sometimes damaging the device permanently. NiMH batteries use a sealed construction with a pressure relief valve. Instead of leaking liquid, an overpressured NiMH cell vents gas. This is one of the strongest practical arguments for switching every device in your household to rechargeables: you stop losing flashlights, remotes, and weather radios to corroded battery compartments.
 Match your sets
 Use identical batteries within each device: same brand, same capacity, same age, same charge state. Mixing different cells in the same device causes uneven discharge, which reduces performance and can over-discharge the weaker cell. Between devices, mix freely. One flashlight on Eneloops and another on EBL is perfectly fine.
 How many to own
 Count every device in your household that runs on AA or AAA batteries. Multiply by the number of cells each device takes. Double the total so you have one set installed and one set charged and stored. A typical household needs 16 to 24 AA cells and 8 to 12 AAA cells. Buy a quality charger with independent slots, charge every set fully, and store the spares in a cool, dry place. Pair these with a set of stored fuel for your generator and you have covered the two most common failure points in a power outage.
 For the full guide on emergency power, portable stations, and solar charging, visit the Energy self-reliance section .
 About the author
 Dan Whelan is the founder of New World Survival. He and his wife Vicki rode out Hurricane Andrew in 1992 and spent the week after sorting donations at a relief center in Homestead. More than thirty years of household preparedness later, he built this site to pass on what works. Read their story

 How we test rechargeable batteries
 We test every rechargeable battery in the Which? test lab using a strict set of criteria to sort the exceptional models from the short-lived.
 How long will the rechargeable batteries last?  We test rechargeable batteries in high-drain conditions to reveal which keep even the most power-hungry devices running for the longest on a single charge. 
 Do the batteries last for as long when recharged multiple times  We recharge and discharge each rechargeable battery hundreds of times in some of the toughest conditions you could use them in at home, such as with a bright LED pocket torch, to reveal which batteries last the distance. We also measure each battery’s capacity over time to find out for how long they can reach at least 80% of their initial capacity, and for how long they can reach 60% of their initial capacity (the point at which you’ll notice you have to recharge them more often).
 How long will rechargeable batteries stay charged  All rechargeable batteries ‘leak away’ their charge over time, so we test this by fully charging eight batteries from each brand on test and then leaving them unused. We measure the power remaining in four batteries after 25 days and in the other four after 50 days.
 Do rechargeable batteries live up to their capacity claims  We measure the capacity of each battery, measured in milliamp hours (mAh), in our lifetime tests and compare it with the capacity stated on the packet. The higher the capacity rating, the longer the batteries should keep your devices powered.
 Which rechargeable batteries charge the fastest  We measure how long each set of batteries takes to charge using our smart charger on the soft-charge (i.e. not super-fast) setting. However, charging time isn't factored into the total test score because it depends directly on the capacity of the rechargeable batteries you choose; smaller-capacity batteries typically charge faster.
 We regularly revisit rechargeable batteries on sale to see if there are any more popular models that need testing, and when we find them, we do so.
 Find out more about how Which? isn't influenced by product manufacturers or retailers, and how your support helps us to stay  editorially independent 
 Battery charger buying tips
 We asked hundreds of Which? members* what's important and useful to them about their battery charger. Read the tips below to help choose the best for you – and avoid purchasing a dud. 
 An indicator to show when the battery is charging or fully charged (60% found this important). 
 How many different battery sizes it can charge (51% found this important). 
 Trickle-charge function. This is especially useful if your batteries have low self-discharge, as it helps with battery longevity (45% found this important). 
 A charger that shows you how much capacity remains. A rechargeable battery's maximum charge naturally decreases over time. 
  *Based on a survey of 1,346 Which? members.  
 Different types of battery chargers
 Smart charger Also known as delta-V chargers, these monitor the voltage levels in each battery and stop charging (or switch to a low trickle-charge setting) when they’re full. They're usually the best choice for keeping rechargeable batteries in good shape because they prevent overcharging, which can reduce battery life. 
 Trickle charger  These push a low ‘trickle’ charge through batteries for a long period of time to help prevent damage and degradation. Some have timers, so they turn off automatically after a set period. This won’t necessarily prevent overcharging or undercharging because the time will vary depending on other factors, such as the battery’s capacity, chemistry and age. Trickle chargers are especially useful if your rechargeable batteries aren’t ‘low self-discharge’ models (which use technology to reduce charge loss when not in use). 
 Other battery chargers If a battery charger isn't marked as a smart charger or trickle charger, it’s likely to be a more basic model that pumps a constant electrical current through batteries until you unplug it. These models are often cheaper, but it can be hard to tell when batteries are fully charged – and the charger won’t stop charging them when they are. This increases the risk of overcharging, which can cause long-term damage. If you leave them unplugged, the batteries could be undercharged or even flat the next time you need them.

 Battery charger speeds
 The type of battery charger that's best for you will depend on how you plan to charge your batteries, and how much you want to spend.
 Super-fast chargers  Battery-charging technology is constantly evolving, and many smart chargers are claimed to charge batteries in under an hour. The fastest models should be able to charge in 15 minutes – which is convenient, as you don’t need to think about charging your batteries before you want to use them. However, they tend to be pricier than other battery chargers. 
 Slower chargers  Manufacturers often state the expected charging time on their battery chargers – for example, both Duracell and Energizer sell a ‘one-hour’ charger, among other models. Exactly how long it will take depends on the capacity of your rechargeable batteries. In the same charger, higher-capacity batteries will take longer to charge than lower-capacity ones. Other chargers are designed to be left charging overnight – some have auto shut-off functions after certain time periods to minimise overcharging.
 Can smoke detectors and other alarms use rechargeable batteries?
 They can, but we wouldn't recommend it because charge retention can be unreliable. For devices like alarms, this could be inconvenient or even dangerous. Matt Stevens, our expert on carbon monoxide, heat and smoke alarms, offers this advice:
 If the alarms in your home (carbon monoxide, heat or smoke) are powered by replaceable batteries, you'll need to use disposables. Rechargeable batteries lose charge faster than disposables making them unsuitable for this critical task. When the batteries are running low, your alarms will chirp regularly to let you know. If changing the batteries isn't a task you're keen on doing, go for an alarm with a sealed battery. For this kind of alarm, the battery will last for the natural lifetime of the alarm itself.

 Based on hours of hands-on testing, the Energizer Recharge Universal AAs are our top pick.  The most important questions with rechargeable batteries are how much charge they can hold and how quickly they can deliver it. So we tested many of the products in this guide by measuring just that, using two high-end chargers (a La Crosse BC700-CBP and a SkyRC MC3000) to measure the amount of charge each battery could hold, testing four of each and averaging the result. We tested AA batteries, as these are the most commonly used size for modern electronics like TV remotes , smart doorbells , and outdoor security cameras .
 To see how long the batteries in our test group would last, we used them to run two devices: a small battery-powered fan and a powerful flashlight. Drawing 0.6 and 1.4 Amps, respectively, these devices allowed us to measure how long each battery can run during low-drain and high-drain use. For these tests, we ran our fan at maximum speed, recording how long it kept rotating. Our flashlight was operated at maximum brightness—roughly 350 lumens—as we recorded how long it stayed lit.
 When the blades stopped turning, the time was noted and the test was stopped. In instances where we had to step away from observing the test, we set up a GoPro camera to record the operation of the fans, just in case one stopped running while we were out of the room.
 How Do Rechargeable Batteries Work?
 Rechargeable batteries are pretty simple devices, but there’s a lot of jargon surrounding them. Here’s our guide to the terms you need to know to make an informed choice. 
 NiMH (nickel-metal hydride battery): One side of a NiMH rechargeable battery is made of Nickel Oxide Hydroxide, and the other is made of an alloy of several rare earth metals. When the battery is charged, the Nickel Oxide Hydroxide gives up a Hydrogen ion, which is absorbed by the alloy. When the battery is used, this is reversed, creating a flow of electric charge outward.
 Lithium-Ion: There are more than a dozen different types of lithium-ion batteries out there, chemically speaking, but the concept is the same. They recharge at least twice as fast as NiMH batteries, and they output a higher voltage than NiMH batteries, so their performance can seem more consistent over a given period of time.
 Charger: the device that controls the flow of charge into a battery. You should never use a NiMH battery (like the ones in this guide) with a non-NiMH charger, as this can damage them. 
 LSD: Low Self-Discharge. All batteries lose a certain amount of charge over time, even when they are not connected to anything. This is called self-discharge.
 Typically, a NiMH battery will lose up to half its charge if stored for a year. Some brands minimize this with extra insulation inside the battery.
 mAh: milliamp-hours. A measure of the amount of charge that can be stored in a battery. 1 mAh is a flow of one milliamp over an hour, so a 2500 mAh battery can deliver 2500 milliamps (or 2.5 Amps) for one hour, or 250 milliamps for 10 hours. 
 Cycles or Recharge Life: Each full charge and discharge is one battery cycle. All batteries lose capacity when used, meaning that they can store a little less juice when fully charged each cycle. Manufacturers offer a cycle life—the estimated number of cycles a battery can go through before it loses a certain amount of its capacity. This is defined in a standard called IEC 61951-2.
 Other Sizes and Adapters: We focused on rechargeable AAs for this guide, as they are by far the most commonly used battery size. They can also be used to power devices that require C and D cells, too. All you have to do is pop them into an appropriately-sized adapter and you’re in business. This adapter set from Eneloop is a great option for anyone interested in doing this.
 How Long Do Rechargeable Batteries Last?
 Depending on how often you use them, and how much you recharge them, rechargeable AA batteries typically last at least two to five years. After a couple of years, you’ll likely start to notice them holding less and less charge with regular use. But they can last as long as seven years or so if you treat them with the utmost care and don’t rely on them constantly. Of course, it depends somewhat on which brand of battery you buy.

 How we test rechargeable batteries
 We test every rechargeable battery in the Which? test lab using a strict set of criteria to sort the exceptional models from the short-lived.
 How long will the rechargeable batteries last?  We test rechargeable batteries in high-drain conditions to reveal which keep even the most power-hungry devices running for the longest on a single charge. 
 Do the batteries last for as long when recharged multiple times  We recharge and discharge each rechargeable battery hundreds of times in some of the toughest conditions you could use them in at home, such as with a bright LED pocket torch, to reveal which batteries last the distance. We also measure each battery’s capacity over time to find out for how long they can reach at least 80% of their initial capacity, and for how long they can reach 60% of their initial capacity (the point at which you’ll notice you have to recharge them more often).
 How long will rechargeable batteries stay charged  All rechargeable batteries ‘leak away’ their charge over time, so we test this by fully charging eight batteries from each brand on test and then leaving them unused. We measure the power remaining in four batteries after 25 days and in the other four after 50 days.
 Do rechargeable batteries live up to their capacity claims  We measure the capacity of each battery, measured in milliamp hours (mAh), in our lifetime tests and compare it with the capacity stated on the packet. The higher the capacity rating, the longer the batteries should keep your devices powered.
 Which rechargeable batteries charge the fastest  We measure how long each set of batteries takes to charge using our smart charger on the soft-charge (i.e. not super-fast) setting. However, charging time isn't factored into the total test score because it depends directly on the capacity of the rechargeable batteries you choose; smaller-capacity batteries typically charge faster.
 We regularly revisit rechargeable batteries on sale to see if there are any more popular models that need testing, and when we find them, we do so.
 Find out more about how Which? isn't influenced by product manufacturers or retailers, and how your support helps us to stay  editorially independent 
 Battery charger buying tips
 We asked hundreds of Which? members* what's important and useful to them about their battery charger. Read the tips below to help choose the best for you – and avoid purchasing a dud. 
 An indicator to show when the battery is charging or fully charged (60% found this important). 
 How many different battery sizes it can charge (51% found this important). 
 Trickle-charge function. This is especially useful if your batteries have low self-discharge, as it helps with battery longevity (45% found this important). 
 A charger that shows you how much capacity remains. A rechargeable battery's maximum charge naturally decreases over time. 
  *Based on a survey of 1,346 Which? members.  
 Different types of battery chargers
 Smart charger Also known as delta-V chargers, these monitor the voltage levels in each battery and stop charging (or switch to a low trickle-charge setting) when they’re full. They're usually the best choice for keeping rechargeable batteries in good shape because they prevent overcharging, which can reduce battery life. 
 Trickle charger  These push a low ‘trickle’ charge through batteries for a long period of time to help prevent damage and degradation. Some have timers, so they turn off automatically after a set period. This won’t necessarily prevent overcharging or undercharging because the time will vary depending on other factors, such as the battery’s capacity, chemistry and age. Trickle chargers are especially useful if your rechargeable batteries aren’t ‘low self-discharge’ models (which use technology to reduce charge loss when not in use). 
 Other battery chargers If a battery charger isn't marked as a smart charger or trickle charger, it’s likely to be a more basic model that pumps a constant electrical current through batteries until you unplug it. These models are often cheaper, but it can be hard to tell when batteries are fully charged – and the charger won’t stop charging them when they are. This increases the risk of overcharging, which can cause long-term damage. If you leave them unplugged, the batteries could be undercharged or even flat the next time you need them.

 Battery charger speeds
 The type of battery charger that's best for you will depend on how you plan to charge your batteries, and how much you want to spend.
 Super-fast chargers  Battery-charging technology is constantly evolving, and many smart chargers are claimed to charge batteries in under an hour. The fastest models should be able to charge in 15 minutes – which is convenient, as you don’t need to think about charging your batteries before you want to use them. However, they tend to be pricier than other battery chargers. 
 Slower chargers  Manufacturers often state the expected charging time on their battery chargers – for example, both Duracell and Energizer sell a ‘one-hour’ charger, among other models. Exactly how long it will take depends on the capacity of your rechargeable batteries. In the same charger, higher-capacity batteries will take longer to charge than lower-capacity ones. Other chargers are designed to be left charging overnight – some have auto shut-off functions after certain time periods to minimise overcharging.
 Can smoke detectors and other alarms use rechargeable batteries?
 They can, but we wouldn't recommend it because charge retention can be unreliable. For devices like alarms, this could be inconvenient or even dangerous. Matt Stevens, our expert on carbon monoxide, heat and smoke alarms, offers this advice:
 If the alarms in your home (carbon monoxide, heat or smoke) are powered by replaceable batteries, you'll need to use disposables. Rechargeable batteries lose charge faster than disposables making them unsuitable for this critical task. When the batteries are running low, your alarms will chirp regularly to let you know. If changing the batteries isn't a task you're keen on doing, go for an alarm with a sealed battery. For this kind of alarm, the battery will last for the natural lifetime of the alarm itself.

 How to choose rechargeable batteries
 Digital Camera World and ZDNet, two technology publications that review batteries, set out what to look at.
 Capacity against how often you recharge. Digital Camera World says standard Eneloop cells hold less per charge than Eneloop Pro cells but can be recharged many more times, and it calls the EBL 2800 mAh cell among the highest-capacity AA options. ZDNet separates high-drain devices such as camera flashguns and game controllers from low-drain ones such as remotes. The EBL AA 2800mAh pack lists 2800 mAh, the Amazon Basics AA 2000 mAh pack lists 2000 mAh, and the Brightown AA batteries list 1000 mAh.
 Low self-discharge. ZDNet says batteries should ideally keep at least 80 percent of their charge after a year of storage, and that low self-discharge cells like Eneloop can hold a charge for months or even years. The Eneloop AAA listing says up to 70 percent after 10 years unused, the EBL AAA 1100mAh listing says 80 percent after 3 years, and the Amazon Basics AA 2000 mAh listing says 80 percent after 2 years.
 Chemistry and voltage. Digital Camera World says NiMH cells deliver 1.2 V, while newer lithium-ion AA cells deliver 1.5 V like alkaline batteries. ZDNet adds that lithium-ion cells can run hotter and need a good smart charger with overcharge protection. All six of our picks are NiMH. Lithium AA cells also appear in Amazon’s results, but none reached our shortlist.
 A charger, and fit. None of the listing text we read for our six picks says a charger is included, so plan to own or buy one. Check fit too: Amazon’s own summary of the EBL AA 2800mAh lists fit as negative and names smoke detectors.
